questions.explanation: Useful segments must be measurable, accessible, substantial, differentiable and actionable. A segment that contains every consumer is not a segment at all, but the whole market. Options C, D and B are standard requirements.

questions.question: A market segment is said to be measurable when

options.a: it can be reached and served effectively
options.b: it responds differently from other segments
options.c: it is large enough to be profitable
options.d: its size, purchasing power and profile can be estimated

questions.explanation: Measurability means the firm can estimate how big the segment is and how much it can buy. Option A describes accessibility. Option C describes substantiality, and option B describes differentiability.

questions.question: A market segment is said to be accessible when

options.a: it has no competitors at all
options.c: the firm can effectively reach and serve it
options.d: it is the largest segment in the market

questions.explanation: Accessibility means the firm can reach the segment through suitable channels and media and can deliver to it. Option B is measurability. Option A is not a requirement; segments often have competitors.

questions.question: A firm finds a group of customers with clear needs, but the group has only a few dozen buyers and would not cover the cost of a separate marketing programme. Which requirement of an effective segment does this group fail?
questions.explanation: A substantial segment is large or profitable enough to be worth serving with its own marketing programme, and a few dozen buyers fail that test. Option A is not the problem, since the group's size is known. Option B is about reaching the buyers, which is not in doubt here.

questions.question: A segment is said to be differentiable when

options.a: it is conceptually distinct and responds differently to marketing mix elements than other segments
options.b: its members all live in the same area
options.c: it is large enough to be profitable
options.d: the firm can reach it through its usual channels

questions.explanation: Differentiable segments are distinct from one another, so a change in the marketing mix produces a different response in each. If two groups respond in the same way, they are not really separate segments. Option C is substantiality and option D is accessibility.

questions.question: A segment is said to be actionable when

options.a: it is large enough to be profitable
options.b: it is distinct from other segments
options.c: the firm can design effective programmes to attract and serve it

questions.explanation: Actionability means the firm has the resources and ability to build a marketing programme that attracts and serves the segment. A small firm may see several attractive segments but lack the staff or money to act on all of them. Options D, B and A describe measurability, differentiability and substantiality.

questions.question: Evaluating the attractiveness of each market segment and selecting one or more segments to enter is called
questions.explanation: Targeting comes after segmentation: the firm compares segments and chooses which to serve. Option D is the earlier step of dividing the market. Option C is the later step of creating a clear place for the product in target customers' minds.

questions.question: Which of the following shows the correct order of the main steps in target marketing?
questions.explanation: A firm first divides the market into segments, then chooses target segments, and then positions its offer in the minds of the chosen buyers. Option C is tempting, but you cannot position a product before deciding whom it is for. Options A and D start with steps that depend on segmentation.

questions.question: A firm that ignores segment differences and targets the whole market with one offer is using
questions.explanation: Undifferentiated or mass marketing treats the market as one group with common needs and uses a single marketing mix. Option B uses separate offers for several segments. Option D focuses on one segment or niche, and option A tailors offers to local groups or individuals.

questions.question: A beverage company sells a low-priced sachet drink for low-income buyers, a premium bottled range for upper-income buyers and a sugar-free version for health-conscious buyers, each with its own advertising. This targeting strategy is
questions.explanation: Serving several segments with a separate product and marketing programme for each is differentiated marketing. Options C and A use one offer for the whole market. Option D focuses on just one segment.

questions.question: When a firm with limited resources goes after a large share of one small segment or niche, it is using
questions.explanation: Concentrated or niche marketing focuses the firm's effort on one segment, allowing it to know that group well and serve it efficiently. Option A serves several segments at once. Option C serves the whole market with one offer.

questions.question: The main risk of a concentrated (niche) targeting strategy is that

options.a: the firm cannot learn about its customers' needs
options.b: its marketing costs are always higher than those of mass marketing
options.c: the firm depends heavily on one segment, so a change in that segment can hurt it badly
options.d: the firm must design many different products at the same time

questions.explanation: Putting all effort into one segment means that a fall in demand or a strong new rival in that segment can seriously damage the firm. Option D is a feature of differentiated marketing. Option A is wrong because a niche firm usually knows its customers very well.

questions.question: Compared with undifferentiated marketing, a key disadvantage of differentiated marketing is that it

options.a: raises the costs of product development, production and promotion

questions.explanation: Running separate products and marketing programmes for several segments usually increases costs, so the firm must check that the extra sales justify them. Option C describes undifferentiated marketing. Option D describes concentrated marketing.

questions.question: Arranging for a product to occupy a clear, distinctive and desirable place relative to competing products in the minds of target consumers is called
questions.explanation: Positioning is about the image and value the target customers associate with a brand compared with rivals. Option C divides the market into groups. Option B selects which groups to serve.

questions.question: A new fast-food chain advertises itself as 'the fastest affordable meal for busy office workers in Lagos'. This statement is mainly an example of

options.b: segmenting the market by geography only
options.c: measuring the size of a segment
options.d: positioning the brand in the minds of its target market

questions.explanation: The slogan tells a chosen target group (busy office workers) what distinct value the brand offers compared with rivals, which is positioning. Option A is wrong because the firm has clearly picked a target group. Option B is only partly present; the main purpose of the statement is to set the brand's place in customers' minds.

questions.question: Which of the following is a major benefit of market segmentation to a firm?

options.a: It removes the need for any market research
options.b: It allows the firm to charge the same price to every buyer
options.c: It guarantees that the firm will have no competitors
options.d: It helps the firm match its products and marketing mix more closely to customers' needs

questions.explanation: By understanding the needs of each group, the firm can design products, prices, distribution and promotion that fit those needs better, which can raise sales and loyalty. Option A is wrong because segmentation depends on research. Option C is wrong because rivals can still target the same segment.

questions.question: From a managerial economics point of view, market segmentation helps a firm to use its resources efficiently mainly because

options.a: it eliminates fixed costs of production
options.b: it allows the firm to spread its budget equally over all consumers
options.c: it can concentrate spending on the segments that offer the best returns
options.d: it makes demand perfectly elastic in every segment

questions.explanation: Segmentation shows where demand, purchasing power and profit potential are greatest, so scarce marketing money goes where it earns most. Option B is the opposite of a targeted approach. Option A is wrong because segmentation does not affect the firm's fixed costs.

questions.question: A cinema charges lower ticket prices to students than to working adults. If the firm separates the two groups and wants to maximise profit, it should charge the higher price to the group whose demand is
questions.explanation: Charging different prices to segments (price discrimination) raises profit when the higher price goes to the group less sensitive to price, since they cut purchases less when price rises. Students usually have more elastic demand, so they get the discount. Option C reverses the rule; raising price for an elastic group cuts sales sharply.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT usually a benefit of market segmentation?

options.a: It helps the firm compete more effectively in chosen segments
options.b: It always lowers the firm's total marketing costs
options.c: It allows better design of the marketing mix
options.d: It helps the firm spot new market opportunities

questions.explanation: Segmentation often increases some costs, because serving different groups needs different products and campaigns, so it does not always lower total marketing costs. Options D, A and C are genuine benefits: spotting unmet needs, focusing competitive effort and fitting the mix to buyers.

questions.question: A campus food delivery start-up estimates that 48,000 students are on campus, that 35% of them order food online, and that each such student spends N2,500 a month on deliveries. What is the estimated monthly value of this segment?
questions.explanation: Segment value = number of buyers x share in the segment x spending per buyer = 48,000 x 0.35 x 2,500 = N42,000,000 a month. Option A forgets that only 35% of students are in the segment. Option C uses the 65% who do not order online, and option B is a yearly figure, not a monthly one.

questions.question: A town has 120,000 households. 40% have monthly incomes above N300,000, and a survey shows 25% of those households want a home-cleaning service. How many households are in this target segment?
questions.explanation: The segment is households that meet both conditions: 120,000 x 0.40 x 0.25 = 12,000 households. Option C stops at the income filter and ignores interest in the service. Option D adds the percentages instead of applying one after the other.

questions.question: Limited liability is a key benefit enjoyed by the owners of:

options.b: all of these types of business

questions.explanation: In a limited liability company, shareholders can lose only what they invested, because the company is a separate legal person responsible for its own debts. Owners in options A and D have unlimited liability, so their personal assets can be used to pay business debts, which also rules out option B.

questions.question: A business that is owned, financed and controlled by one person, who takes all the profit and bears all the risk, is a
questions.explanation: A sole proprietorship has a single owner who provides the capital, makes the decisions, keeps all the profit and bears all the losses. Option D has two or more owners. Options B and A are owned by shareholders and by government respectively.

questions.question: Which of the following is a typical advantage of a sole proprietorship?

options.b: Easy access to large amounts of capital
options.c: Continuity of the business after the owner's death
options.d: Quick decision-making because the owner does not need to consult anyone

questions.explanation: The sole trader makes decisions alone, so the business can respond quickly to customers and changes in the market. Option A is wrong because the sole trader has unlimited liability. Options B and C are actually weaknesses of this form: capital is limited and the business may end with the owner.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a disadvantage of a sole proprietorship?

options.c: The owner keeps all the profits

questions.explanation: Keeping all the profit is an advantage, since the owner does not share it with anyone. Options A, D and B are well-known drawbacks: personal assets can be lost, the business may end with the owner's death or illness, and one person can raise only limited capital.

questions.question: Mama Bisi runs a provision shop alone. The shop fails and owes suppliers N2 million, which is more than the shop's assets are worth. Creditors take her personal car to recover the debt. This shows that a sole proprietor has
questions.explanation: Unlimited liability means the owner is personally responsible for all business debts, so private assets can be taken to pay them. Option C would protect her personal assets. Options A and D are features of a registered company, which exists separately from its owners.

questions.question: The most common way for a sole proprietor in Nigeria to raise starting capital is

options.a: personal savings and loans from family and friends
options.b: grants voted by the National Assembly
options.c: selling debentures on the stock exchange
options.d: issuing shares to the general public

questions.explanation: A one-person business usually starts with the owner's savings, help from relatives and friends, and later small bank loans or trade credit. Options D and C are open only to public limited companies. Option B applies to government-owned enterprises.

questions.question: One reason the sole proprietorship is the most common form of business in Nigeria is that it

options.a: can sell its shares on the stock exchange
options.b: must have at least two directors
options.d: is easy and cheap to set up, with few legal formalities

questions.explanation: Starting a sole proprietorship needs little capital and few formalities, which suits petty trading and small services. Option C is wrong because the owner has unlimited liability. Options A and B describe companies, not one-person businesses.

questions.question: The relationship between persons carrying on a business in common with a view of profit, who share capital, management and profits, is called
questions.explanation: A partnership is formed when two or more people agree to run a business together and share its profits. Option A has only one owner. Option D is owned by government, and option C is owned by members mainly to serve their own needs rather than for profit.

questions.question: A deed of partnership is

options.a: a share certificate given to each partner
options.b: the written agreement that sets out the rights, duties and profit-sharing arrangements of the partners
options.c: a loan document issued to partnership creditors
options.d: the certificate that makes a partnership a separate legal person

questions.explanation: The partnership deed records matters such as capital contributed, profit-sharing ratio, duties of partners and how disputes or admission of new partners are handled. Option D is wrong because an ordinary partnership does not become a separate legal person. Option A describes companies, which issue shares.

questions.question: Chidi contributes N5 million to a partnership business but takes no part in running it, while his partners manage it daily. Chidi is best described as a
questions.explanation: A sleeping or dormant partner contributes capital and shares profit but does not take part in managing the business. Option D lends only their name and reputation, usually without contributing capital. Option C is involved in day-to-day management.

questions.question: A partner who allows his name to be used by the firm to give it credibility, but who contributes no capital and takes no part in management, is a
questions.explanation: A nominal partner lends only their name and reputation to the firm. Option A contributes capital but does not manage. Option B contributes capital with liability limited to that capital.

questions.question: In a limited partnership, a limited partner

options.a: can never share in the profits of the firm
options.b: is liable only up to the capital contributed and does not take part in managing the business
options.c: must manage the business on behalf of other partners
options.d: is personally liable for all debts of the firm

questions.explanation: A limited partner's risk is limited to the capital put in, and in return they do not take part in management. Option D describes a general partner. Option A is wrong because limited partners do share profits.

questions.question: In an ordinary (general) partnership, the liability of the partners for the debts of the firm is

options.a: borne only by the most senior partner
options.b: limited to the value of their shares
options.c: unlimited, so partners' private assets can be used to pay the firm's debts
options.d: limited to the amount of their capital contributions

questions.explanation: General partners are jointly liable for the firm's debts without limit, just like a sole proprietor. Options D and B describe limited partners and company shareholders. Option A is wrong because liability is shared by all general partners.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an advantage of a partnership over a sole proprietorship?

options.a: More capital can be raised from several owners
options.b: Each partner can be bound by the actions of the other partners
options.c: Partners can share skills and specialise

questions.explanation: The fact that one partner's business actions bind all the others is a risk, not an advantage, and it can lead to losses or disputes. Options A, C and D are genuine gains from having more than one owner.

questions.question: Three friends run a law firm as a partnership without any special continuation clause. One of them dies. In general, the partnership is

options.b: converted automatically into a public limited company
options.c: unaffected, because it has perpetual succession
options.d: dissolved, though the remaining partners may form a new one

questions.explanation: An ordinary partnership lacks continuity: the death, bankruptcy or withdrawal of a partner generally ends the existing agreement. Option C describes a registered company, which continues whatever happens to its members. Options B and A have no basis in law.

questions.question: The right of a registered company to continue in existence even when its shareholders die or sell their shares is called
questions.explanation: Perpetual succession means the company's life does not depend on its members, because it exists as a separate legal person. Option A concerns how much shareholders can lose, not how long the company lasts. Option C is a feature of sole traders and general partners.

questions.question: The phrase 'a company is a separate legal entity' means that

options.a: the owners are personally responsible for all company debts
options.b: the company is owned and controlled by the government
options.c: the company can own property, sue and be sued in its own name, apart from its owners
options.d: the company can only be formed by one person

questions.explanation: Once registered, a company is a legal person distinct from its shareholders, so it holds assets, enters contracts and goes to court in its own name. Option B describes a public enterprise. Option A describes unlimited liability, which is the opposite of the protection a company gives.

questions.question: Ade owns 10,000 fully paid shares in a limited company that goes into liquidation owing large debts. What is the most Ade can lose?

options.a: Nothing at all, because shares are always refunded
options.c: Twice the value of his shares
options.d: The amount he paid for his shares

questions.explanation: Shareholders in a limited liability company can lose at most what they invested in (or still owe on) their shares; their private property is protected. Option B describes unlimited liability. Option A is wrong because shares can become worthless when a company fails.

questions.question: Which of the following is the key difference between a private limited company (Ltd) and a public limited company (Plc)?

options.a: A Plc has no separate legal personality, while an Ltd does
options.b: Shareholders of an Ltd have unlimited liability, while those of a Plc have limited liability
options.c: A Plc can invite the general public to buy its shares, while an Ltd cannot
options.d: An Ltd is owned by government, while a Plc is owned by individuals

questions.explanation: The main distinction is that a public company may offer its shares to the public and have them traded on the stock exchange, while a private company restricts the transfer of its shares and cannot invite the public to subscribe. Option B is wrong because both have limited liability. Option A is wrong because both are separate legal entities.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of a private limited company?

options.b: It restricts the right to transfer its shares
options.c: Its shares are freely sold to the public on the stock exchange
options.d: It has a separate legal identity

questions.explanation: A private company may not invite the public to buy its shares, so they are not traded on the stock exchange. Options A, D and B are all features of a private limited company.

questions.question: Which of the following is a major advantage of a public limited company?

options.a: It can be formed quickly with very few legal formalities
options.b: It can raise very large amounts of capital from the public
options.c: Its affairs can be kept completely secret
options.d: The owners always manage the business directly

questions.explanation: Selling shares and debentures to the public lets a Plc raise far more capital than a sole trader, partnership or private company. Option A is wrong because forming a public company involves many formalities. Option C is wrong because a Plc must disclose a great deal of information, and option D because ownership and management are often separate.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a common disadvantage of a public limited company?

options.a: Shareholders have unlimited liability for its debts
options.b: It must disclose much of its financial information to the public
options.d: Formation is costly and involves many legal requirements

questions.explanation: Shareholders of a Plc have limited liability, so option A is not a disadvantage of this form at all. Options C, D and B are real drawbacks: managers may pursue their own aims, formation is expensive, and much of its information must be made public.

questions.question: In Nigeria, the body responsible for registering companies and issuing certificates of incorporation is the
questions.explanation: The Corporate Affairs Commission registers businesses and companies and issues the certificate of incorporation that gives a company its legal existence. Option C regulates banks and monetary policy. Option B collects federal taxes.

questions.question: The memorandum of association of a company is the document that

options.a: sets out the internal rules for running the company's meetings and management
options.b: sets out the company's name, objects and relationship with the outside world
options.c: records the daily cash sales of the company
options.d: is the contract between the company and its bankers

questions.explanation: The memorandum is the company's charter, stating basic facts such as its name, objects and liability of members, and governing its external relationships. Option A describes the articles of association, which cover internal rules. Options C and D are routine business records, not formation documents.

questions.question: Which statement correctly compares ordinary shareholders and debenture holders of a company?

options.a: Ordinary shareholders are owners who receive variable dividends, while debenture holders are creditors who receive fixed interest
options.b: Both receive a fixed rate of interest whether or not the company makes a profit
options.c: Ordinary shareholders are paid first when a company is wound up
options.d: Debenture holders are owners with voting rights, while ordinary shareholders are creditors

questions.explanation: Ordinary shares give part-ownership, voting rights and dividends that depend on profit, while debentures are long-term loans that earn fixed interest. Option D reverses the two roles. Option C is wrong because creditors, including debenture holders, are paid before ordinary shareholders.

questions.question: Which of the following is a form of internal finance for a limited company?
questions.explanation: Retained earnings are profits kept in the business instead of being paid out as dividends, so the money comes from within the firm. Options B, A and D all bring in money from outside investors or lenders.

questions.question: Shares that carry a fixed rate of dividend and are paid before ordinary shareholders, but usually carry limited voting rights, are
questions.explanation: Preference shareholders get a fixed dividend and priority over ordinary shareholders for dividends and repayment of capital. Option D carries variable dividends and full voting rights. Option A is a loan, not a share.

questions.question: A business organisation that is established by an Act of the legislature, owned and financed by government, and run by a board appointed by government to provide essential services, is a
questions.explanation: A public corporation is created by statute and owned by the state, mainly to provide essential services in the public interest. Option C sounds similar, but a Plc is owned by private shareholders who buy its shares. Options A and B are private-sector businesses.

questions.question: Which of the following is a main reason governments set up public enterprises?

options.a: To reduce the supply of basic infrastructure
options.b: To avoid any form of accountability to the public
options.c: To maximise dividends paid to private shareholders
options.d: To provide essential services that private firms may not provide adequately or at affordable prices

questions.explanation: Governments often run strategic or essential services, such as utilities, transport and ports, where huge capital is needed or the public interest matters more than profit. Option C describes the goal of private companies. Option B is wrong because public enterprises answer to government and the legislature.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a common problem of public enterprises in Nigeria?

options.a: Excessive pressure from private shareholders to pay dividends
options.c: Inefficiency and dependence on government subsidies

questions.explanation: Public enterprises are owned by government, not private shareholders, so dividend pressure from private owners is not their problem. Options B, D and C are frequently cited weaknesses that led to calls for privatisation and commercialisation.

questions.question: What is the difference between privatisation and commercialisation of a public enterprise?

options.a: Privatisation transfers ownership to private investors, while commercialisation keeps government ownership but requires the enterprise to run on profit-oriented lines
options.b: Both mean that the government closes the enterprise down
options.c: Privatisation applies only to partnerships and commercialisation only to sole proprietorships
options.d: Privatisation keeps government ownership, while commercialisation sells the enterprise to private investors

questions.explanation: Privatisation sells all or part of the government's stake to private owners, while a commercialised enterprise stays in government hands but must operate efficiently and cover its costs. Option D reverses the two terms. Option B confuses both with liquidation.

questions.question: The main source of capital for a public corporation is

options.a: government funding through budget allocations, grants and loans
options.b: contributions from partners under a deed
options.c: personal savings of its managing director
options.d: sale of ordinary shares to the general public

questions.explanation: Because it is owned by the state, a public corporation is financed mainly by government allocations, grants and government-backed loans, plus any revenue it earns. Option D is how a Plc raises capital. Options C and B apply to sole proprietorships and partnerships.

questions.question: Which of the following pairs of business forms both give their owners limited liability?

options.b: Ordinary partnership and public limited company
options.c: Private limited company and public limited company
options.d: Sole proprietorship and private limited company

questions.explanation: Both private and public limited companies protect shareholders' personal assets, since liability is limited to their shares. Option A lists two forms with unlimited liability. Options D and B each pair a limited company with a form whose owners have unlimited liability.

questions.question: The traditional (neoclassical) theory of the firm assumes that the main objective of the firm is to

options.a: achieve satisfactory rather than maximum results
options.b: maximise profit by producing where marginal revenue equals marginal cost
options.c: maximise sales revenue subject to a minimum profit
options.d: maximise the size of the management staff

questions.explanation: Traditional theory sees the firm as run by an owner-entrepreneur who aims at maximum profit, reached where MR = MC. Option C is the sales revenue maximisation model. Option A describes satisficing in the behavioural theory.

questions.question: Managerial theories of the firm developed mainly because in large modern companies

options.a: ownership by shareholders is separated from control by professional managers
options.b: there are no shareholders at all
options.c: the owner always manages the business personally
options.d: firms have perfect information about all costs and demand

questions.explanation: When shareholders own the firm but salaried managers control it, managers may pursue their own goals, such as sales, growth or status, instead of maximum profit. Option C describes the owner-managed firm of traditional theory. Option D is an assumption of traditional theory that managerial theories question.

questions.question: The model in which managers aim to make total sales revenue as large as possible, provided profit does not fall below the minimum level that keeps shareholders satisfied, is the

options.d: growth of the public sector model

questions.explanation: In the sales revenue maximisation model, managers prefer higher sales because their pay and prestige are linked to the firm's size, subject to a minimum profit constraint. Option A aims at maximum profit with no such trade-off. Option B describes firms seeking satisfactory levels across several goals.

questions.question: Managers of a large Plc spend heavily on extra staff, luxury official cars and large offices because these raise their own satisfaction and status, as long as profits stay acceptable to shareholders. This behaviour is best explained by
questions.explanation: Managerial utility theory says managers maximise their own satisfaction through spending on staff, perks and discretionary investment, subject to a minimum profit. Option B would cut such spending to raise profit. Option C is a production law, not a theory of managers' goals.

questions.question: In the behavioural theory of the firm, 'satisficing' means that the firm

options.c: aims at satisfactory levels of performance rather than the maximum possible
options.d: aims to produce at zero cost

questions.explanation: Satisficing means setting acceptable targets for profit, sales, market share and other goals, because information is limited and many groups must be satisfied. Option B is the traditional assumption. Option A is a managerial model with one main goal.

questions.question: The behavioural theory of the firm views the firm as

options.a: a firm that always has perfect information
options.b: a coalition of groups, such as managers, workers, shareholders and customers, with different and often conflicting goals
options.c: a single owner with one clear goal of maximum profit
options.d: a government agency that ignores costs

questions.explanation: Behavioural theory treats the firm as a coalition whose goals come from bargaining among its groups, so it pursues several targets and settles for satisfactory results. Option C describes the traditional view. Option A contradicts the behavioural idea that information and rationality are limited.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an assumption of the traditional profit maximisation theory of the firm?

options.a: The firm is a coalition of groups that settles for satisfactory results
options.b: The firm is managed by its owner-entrepreneur
options.c: The firm has a single goal of maximum profit
options.d: The firm has full knowledge of its costs and revenues

questions.explanation: The coalition and satisficing idea belongs to the behavioural theory, not the traditional theory. Options B, C and D are standard assumptions of the profit maximisation model.

questions.question: A managerial theory which holds that managers aim mainly at the fastest possible expansion of the firm, subject to keeping the firm safe from takeover, is the
questions.explanation: Growth maximisation theory argues that managers gain power, pay and security when the firm grows, so they pursue the highest sustainable rate of growth while keeping the share price high enough to avoid takeover. Option B is the traditional single-goal model. Option C focuses on the level of sales revenue in a period rather than the growth of the firm over time.

questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of a perfectly competitive market?

options.a: Firms can enter and exit the market freely
options.c: There are few sellers in the market

questions.explanation: Perfect competition has no barriers to entry or exit, so option A is right. Option B is wrong because firms are price takers, and option C is wrong because there are many sellers. Option D describes monopolistic competition, since products in perfect competition are homogeneous.

questions.question: If a perfectly competitive firm is producing where price is greater than marginal cost, it:

options.a: Will increase its profits by producing more
options.c: Will increase its profits by producing less

questions.explanation: When price exceeds marginal cost, each extra unit adds more to revenue than to cost, so producing more raises profit until P = MC, option A. Option C is the opposite. Options B and D cannot be concluded, because whether profit is positive or negative depends on price compared with average total cost, not marginal cost.

questions.question: When firms have an incentive to exit a competitive market, their exit will:

options.a: Drive down the profits of the firms that remain
options.b: Leave market price and output unchanged
options.c: Decrease the quantity of goods supplied in the market

questions.explanation: When firms leave, market supply falls, so the quantity supplied decreases, option C. The lower supply pushes price up, not down, so option D is wrong, and the higher price raises the profits of the remaining firms, which rules out option A. Option B ignores the fall in supply.

questions.question: In a perfectly competitive market, the process of entry or exit of firms ends when:

options.a: Firms are making zero economic profit
options.b: Price is equal to marginal cost
options.c: Firms are operating with excess capacity

questions.explanation: Entry happens while firms earn economic profit and exit happens while they make losses, so the movement stops when economic profit is zero, option A. Option B is true for a competitive firm at every profit-maximising output, even while profits are still attracting entry, so it is not what ends the process. Option D is wrong because marginal revenue equals the constant market price.

questions.question: Compared with other market structures, the equilibrium quantity in an oligopoly market is usually:

options.a: Higher than in monopoly and lower than in perfect competition
options.b: Lower than in both monopoly and perfect competition
options.c: Higher than in both monopoly and perfect competition
options.d: Lower than in monopoly and higher than in perfect competition

questions.explanation: An oligopoly has a few interdependent firms with some market power, so output usually falls between the restricted output of a monopoly and the large output of perfect competition, option A. Option D reverses the order, and options B and C put oligopoly outside the range set by the two extreme structures.

questions.question: A group of firms producing similar or identical products is called:
questions.explanation: An industry, option B, is the aggregate of all firms producing the same or similar products, for example the cement industry. Option A is a single production unit of a firm. Option D is a group of firms that agree to fix prices or output, and option C is a market with only one buyer.

questions.question: Which of the following cannot be classed as a market structure?
questions.explanation: Communism is an economic and political system for organising a whole society, not a way of classifying an industry by its degree of competition. Options C, A and B are all market structures, distinguished by things like the number of firms and how similar their products are.

questions.question: A market structure in which a small number of firms account for most or all of the industry's output is called:
questions.explanation: In an oligopoly a few firms dominate the industry, and each firm's actions affect the others, so they are interdependent. Options A and D have a large number of firms, while option C has only one firm.

questions.question: Which pair of factors is most important in classifying market structures by the nature of competition?

options.a: The size of the firms' offices and their staff strength
options.b: The firms' accounting methods and year-end dates
options.c: The age of the firms and their location
options.d: The number of firms and the degree of product differentiation

questions.explanation: Market structures are told apart mainly by how many sellers there are and how similar or different their products are, for example many firms with identical products in perfect competition or one firm in monopoly. Options C, A and B are business details that do not define the degree of competition.

questions.question: When the minimum efficient scale of production is very large relative to total market demand, the industry is most likely to have:

options.a: no barriers to entry at all
options.b: a very large number of small firms, as in perfect competition
options.c: only one or a few firms, as in monopoly or oligopoly

questions.explanation: If a firm must produce a large share of total market output to reach its lowest average cost, the market can support only one or a few efficient producers, which is why economies of scale can give rise to monopoly. Options B and D need many firms, and option A ignores the cost advantage large firms enjoy.

questions.question: A profit-maximising firm will choose the level of output at which:

options.c: average cost is at its minimum
options.d: total revenue is at its maximum

questions.explanation: Profit is maximised where producing one more unit adds as much to revenue as it adds to cost (MR = MC), so the decision depends on both demand and costs. Option D maximises sales revenue, not profit, and option C gives the most efficient output, which need not be the most profitable one.

questions.question: A perfectly competitive firm will maximise profit at the quantity at which the firm's marginal revenue equals:
questions.explanation: Profit is maximised where marginal revenue equals marginal cost (MR = MC): producing one more unit beyond that point would add more to cost than to revenue. Option D compares a marginal figure with a total figure, which is not the profit rule. Option B has nothing to do with the output decision, since fixed costs do not change with output.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a valid option for a perfectly competitive firm?

options.d: Increasing its price above the market price

questions.explanation: A perfectly competitive firm is a price taker: the price is fixed by market demand and supply, and if it charges more, buyers simply move to the many other sellers of the identical product. It can still change how much it produces, as in options A and B. Option C is also open to it because there are no barriers to exit.

questions.question: In the long run, a perfectly competitive firm will achieve all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: With free entry, any economic profit attracts new firms, which pushes price down until firms earn only normal profit in the long run. At that point price equals marginal cost and minimum average cost, so the firm is allocatively and productively efficient, which is why options D and B are achieved. Option C, normal profit, is exactly what remains in the long run.

questions.question: If the price a firm receives for its product is equal to the marginal cost of producing it, the firm is:
questions.explanation: Allocative efficiency means price (what buyers value the last unit at) equals marginal cost (what it costs to make that unit), so resources go where consumers value them most. Option C is a different idea: productive efficiency means producing at the lowest average cost. Options A and D cannot be read from P = MC alone, because profit depends on average cost.

questions.question: A firm that is producing at the lowest possible average cost is:

options.a: dominating the other firms in the market

questions.explanation: Productive efficiency means producing output at the minimum average cost, so no resources are wasted in making it. Option B is a different concept: allocative efficiency is about price equalling marginal cost. Option C is wrong because a firm at minimum average cost may earn only normal profit if price equals that cost.

questions.question: Which of the following is the best example of a nearly perfectly competitive market?
questions.explanation: Farming comes closest to perfect competition: there are very many small farmers selling an almost identical product, and none of them can change the market price. Option A is controlled by a few big producers, while options C and B are dominated by brands with differentiated products and heavy advertising.

questions.question: Perfect competition is an industry with:

options.b: a few firms producing goods that differ somewhat in quality
options.c: a few firms producing identical goods
options.d: many firms producing goods that differ somewhat

questions.explanation: Perfect competition has a large number of firms selling a homogeneous product, so no single firm can influence the price. Option D describes monopolistic competition, where products are differentiated. Options C and B describe oligopoly, where only a few firms operate.

questions.question: In a perfectly competitive industry, there are:

options.b: one firm that sets the price for the others to follow
options.c: many sellers, but possibly only one or two buyers
options.d: many buyers, but possibly only one or two sellers

questions.explanation: Perfect competition needs large numbers on both sides of the market, so no single buyer or seller can affect the price. Option C describes monopsony or duopsony, where one or two buyers dominate. Option D describes monopoly or duopoly, and option B describes price leadership, which belongs to oligopoly.

questions.question: In perfect competition, the product of a single firm:

options.a: has many perfect complements produced by other firms
options.b: is sold under many different brand names
options.c: has many perfect substitutes produced by other firms
options.d: is sold to different customers at different prices

questions.explanation: Because all firms sell a homogeneous product, each firm's output can be replaced exactly by another firm's output, so it has many perfect substitutes. Option D is price discrimination, which a price taker cannot practise. Option B is wrong because branding is a form of product differentiation, which does not exist in perfect competition.

questions.question: In perfect competition, restrictions on entry into the industry:

options.b: apply to capital but not to labour
options.c: apply to labour but not to capital
options.d: apply to both capital and labour

questions.explanation: One of the defining features of perfect competition is free entry and exit: firms can join or leave the industry without any barriers or government restrictions. Options C, D and B all describe some kind of barrier to entry, which is a feature of monopoly and oligopoly instead.

questions.question: In the long run, monopolistically competitive firms tend to earn:
questions.explanation: Entry into monopolistic competition is free, so short-run profits attract new firms with close substitutes, which takes customers away until only normal profit is left. Option C cannot last because of that entry. Options D and B cannot last either, because loss-making firms leave the industry until the remaining firms break even.

questions.question: For a monopolist, marginal revenue is:
questions.explanation: A monopolist faces a downward-sloping demand curve, so to sell one more unit it must lower the price on all the units it sells. That makes the extra revenue from the last unit smaller than its price. Option A is true only for a price taker in perfect competition, and option B says the same thing as A, since average revenue equals price.

questions.question: Which statement best describes perfect competition?

options.a: It is a theoretical model whose strict assumptions rarely all hold in real-world markets
options.b: It exists wherever the government regulates prices
options.c: It describes markets dominated by a few large firms
options.d: It is the most common market structure in modern economies

questions.explanation: Perfect competition assumes many firms, identical products, perfect knowledge and completely free entry and exit, and real markets rarely meet all of these at once, so it serves mainly as a benchmark. Option D is wrong because most real markets have some product differentiation or market power. Option C describes oligopoly.

questions.question: Monopolistic competition is a market structure characterised by:

options.a: a few large firms whose decisions are interdependent
options.b: a large number of firms selling differentiated products that are close substitutes
options.c: a single firm selling a product with no close substitutes
options.d: many firms selling an identical product

questions.explanation: In monopolistic competition there are many buyers and sellers, but each firm's product is slightly different from its rivals', for example through branding, quality or design, though they remain close substitutes. Option C is monopoly, option A is oligopoly, and option D is perfect competition, where products are homogeneous.

questions.question: The demand curve facing a monopolist is:

options.a: downward sloping, so it can sell more only by lowering its price
options.b: perfectly elastic (horizontal) at the market price
options.c: upward sloping, so it sells more at higher prices

questions.explanation: Because the monopolist is the whole industry, it faces the market demand curve, which slopes downward: a higher price means fewer sales, and selling more means cutting the price. Option B describes a price-taking firm in perfect competition. Option D would mean buyers ignore price completely, which does not happen across all prices.

questions.question: A monopoly is a market structure in which there is:

options.c: only one seller of a product with no close substitutes
options.d: only one buyer of a product

questions.explanation: In a monopoly a single firm makes up the whole industry and sells to many buyers, and it is protected by barriers to entry such as patents, licences or control of raw materials. Option B is a duopoly. Option D is a monopsony, where the single party is the buyer, not the seller. Option A is monopolistic competition.

questions.question: A perfectly competitive firm's short-run supply curve is the part of its marginal cost curve that lies above the:

options.a: minimum point of the average variable cost curve
options.b: maximum point of the average variable cost curve
options.c: maximum point of the total revenue curve
options.d: minimum point of the average fixed cost curve

questions.explanation: Below the lowest point of average variable cost, the price would not cover variable costs and the firm would shut down, so it supplies nothing there. Above that point, the firm produces where price equals marginal cost, which makes the marginal cost curve its supply curve. Option B is wrong because the AVC curve is U-shaped and has a minimum, not a maximum. Option D is wrong because average fixed cost keeps falling and has no minimum.

questions.question: An agreement among firms to fix prices and quantities is known as:
questions.explanation: Collusion is when rival firms, usually in an oligopoly, agree with each other on prices or output instead of competing. Option A, price leadership, is when one firm sets a price and others follow without a formal agreement on quantities. Option B is a tool for analysing strategic decisions, not an agreement.

questions.question: A group of firms that comes together formally to make joint price and output decisions is called:
questions.explanation: A cartel is a formal collusive organisation of firms, such as OPEC, which agree on prices, output or market shares to act like a single monopolist. Option A is the market structure in which cartels usually form, not the group itself. Option B involves one firm leading on price without a formal joint decision.

questions.question: Products produced by oligopolistic firms are:
questions.explanation: Oligopoly can be pure, where a few firms sell a nearly identical product such as cement or petroleum, or differentiated, where a few firms sell branded products such as cars or soft drinks. That is why options C and A are each only half right. Option D is wrong because oligopolists' products are substitutes for one another.

questions.question: A key feature that distinguishes oligopoly is:

options.a: a large number of small price-taking firms
options.c: free entry and exit of firms
options.d: interdependence, because each firm's price and output decisions affect its rivals

questions.explanation: With only a few firms in the market, each one must consider how its rivals will react before changing its price or output, so the firms are interdependent. Option B is common to firms in every market structure. Options A and C describe perfect competition, while oligopoly has a small number of firms and high barriers to entry.

questions.question: Oligopoly is characterised by all of the following EXCEPT:

options.b: a complete absence of rivalry among firms

questions.explanation: In oligopoly, rivalry is intense: each of the few firms watches and reacts to the others, which is why advertising and strategic moves matter so much. A complete absence of rivalry is a feature of perfect competition, where firms are too small to affect each other. Options D, A and C are all standard features of oligopoly.

questions.question: Under the kinked demand curve theory, oligopoly prices are predicted to be:
questions.explanation: The kinked demand model assumes rivals match a price cut but ignore a price rise, so a firm loses sales if it raises price and gains little if it cuts it, and it prefers to leave price unchanged. Option D is the opposite of what the model predicts. Option C is the perfect competition result, not an oligopoly one.

questions.question: In a perfectly contestable market, large oligopolistic firms end up behaving like:
questions.explanation: A contestable market is one where entry and exit are free and costless, so even a few large firms face the constant threat of hit-and-run entry. To keep entrants away they charge prices close to average cost and earn only normal profit, just as perfectly competitive firms do. Options D and B describe firms that can keep prices high, which the threat of entry prevents.

questions.question: Other things equal, and with firms selling identical products, which type of oligopoly competition would you expect to give the highest market output?
questions.explanation: In the Bertrand model, firms selling identical products compete on price and keep undercutting each other until price falls to marginal cost, giving the competitive level of output. Cournot and Stackelberg firms compete on quantity and keep price above marginal cost, so options C and A give less output. Option B, collusion, restricts output the most to raise price.

questions.question: A profit-maximising oligopolistic firm produces at the output level where:
questions.explanation: Every profit-maximising firm, whatever its market structure, chooses the output where marginal revenue equals marginal cost. Option D, price equal to average total cost, is the break-even point where only normal profit is earned. Options B and C do not compare the right quantities for a profit decision.

questions.question: Cartels are most likely to arise in which of the following market structures?
questions.explanation: A cartel needs a small number of firms that can agree and monitor one another, which is exactly the situation in oligopoly. Options A and B have too many firms for an agreement to work. Option C has only one firm, so there is nobody to collude with.

questions.question: Which of the following is a model of NON-collusive oligopoly?
questions.explanation: Non-collusive models assume oligopolists act independently while guessing how rivals will react; the kinked demand curve model and the Cournot model are the classic examples. Options A, D and C all involve firms agreeing with one another on prices, output or market shares, which is collusion.

questions.question: The petroleum industry is an example of:
questions.explanation: A pure oligopoly is a market with a few large firms selling a largely identical product, and crude oil and petroleum products are a standard example. Option B applies to industries like cars, where the few firms sell branded, different products. Option A needs many small firms, and option C needs exactly two.

questions.question: The kinked demand curve model assumes that rivals:

options.a: ignore both price increases and price cuts
options.b: match both price increases and price cuts
options.c: match price cuts but do not match price increases
options.d: match price increases but not price cuts

questions.explanation: The kink comes from asymmetric reactions: if one firm cuts its price, rivals cut too so they do not lose customers, but if it raises its price, rivals keep theirs and take its customers. Option D reverses this. Options B and A would give a smooth demand curve with no kink.

questions.question: The classification of industries according to the degree and nature of competition among the firms operating in them is known as
questions.explanation: Market structure describes how industries differ in the degree and nature of competition, for example in the number of firms, type of product and ease of entry. Option A divides buyers into groups. Option C is the point where demand equals supply.

questions.question: A market with a complete absence of rivalry among firms, a large number of buyers and sellers, homogeneous products and perfect knowledge of the market is
questions.explanation: These are the defining features of perfect competition: many buyers and sellers, identical products, perfect knowledge and no rivalry because no firm can affect price. Option A has many firms but differentiated products. Options C and D have few firms that react to each other's actions.

questions.question: In perfect competition, firms are described as price takers because

options.a: the government fixes the price for every product
options.b: the price is set by market demand and supply, and no single firm can alter it
options.c: firms agree among themselves on a common price
options.d: each firm sets its own price to maximise profit

questions.explanation: Under perfect competition, the equilibrium price comes from the price mechanism, the interaction of market demand and supply, and each firm is too small to influence it. Option D describes a price maker such as a monopolist. Option C describes collusion, which is linked to oligopoly.

questions.question: Under perfect competition, the demand curve facing an individual firm is

options.c: downward sloping, like the market demand curve
options.d: perfectly elastic (horizontal) at the market price

questions.explanation: Because the firm is a price taker, it can sell any quantity at the market price but nothing above it, so its demand curve is horizontal and P = AR = MR. Option C describes firms with some price-setting power, such as a monopolist. Option A is associated with the kinked-demand model of oligopoly.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of a perfectly competitive market?

options.a: A single firm cannot alter the market price
options.b: No barriers to entry into or exit from the market
options.c: Firms differentiate their products through branding
options.d: The exit of one firm has no influence on price

questions.explanation: Products under perfect competition are homogeneous, so there is no room for product differentiation or branding. Options B, A and D are all features of perfect competition.

questions.question: In a large market, thousands of farmers sell identical tomatoes to thousands of buyers who know every seller's price, and anyone can start or stop farming freely. If one farmer tries to sell above the market price, he sells nothing. This market is closest to
questions.explanation: Many sellers and buyers, an identical product, full information and free entry and exit make this close to perfect competition, where each seller is a price taker. Option A has one seller. Option B has one buyer, while here there are thousands.

questions.question: In the long run under perfect competition, if firms are earning supernormal profits, what happens?

options.a: Each firm raises its price to protect its profit
options.b: Firms leave the industry, raising the price further
options.c: The government stops new firms from entering
options.d: New firms enter, market supply rises and price falls until only normal profit is earned

questions.explanation: With free entry, supernormal profit attracts new firms, which increases supply and pushes price down until price equals minimum average cost and only normal profit remains. Option B is what happens when firms are making losses. Option A is impossible because each firm is a price taker.

questions.question: A market in which a single firm makes up the whole industry and sells to many buyers is a
questions.explanation: A monopoly has one seller, so the firm is the industry and serves many buyers. Option C is the reverse case of one buyer facing many sellers. Option B has two dominant sellers.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly describes a monopolist's pricing power?

options.a: It must accept the price set by its rivals
options.b: It cannot change its price without government approval

questions.explanation: A monopolist faces the whole market demand curve and has no close rivals, so it chooses its price (or output) and is a price maker. Option D describes firms in perfect competition. Option A assumes rivals exist, which is not the case in pure monopoly.

questions.question: When a monopolist sells the same product at different prices to different buyers for reasons not related to cost differences, it is practising
questions.explanation: Price discrimination means charging different buyers different prices for the same product, which a monopolist can do because it controls supply. Option B is where one oligopoly firm sets a price that others follow. Option A is about making products distinct, not pricing.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a cause of monopoly?

options.a: Ownership of a strategic raw material
options.c: A very large number of firms selling identical products

questions.explanation: Many firms selling identical products is the opposite of monopoly; it describes perfect competition. Options B, A and D are classic barriers that allow one firm to become or remain the only seller.

questions.question: A pharmaceutical company in Nigeria is the only firm legally allowed to produce a new drug for 20 years because it holds the exclusive right to the invention. Its monopoly arises mainly from

options.b: ownership of a strategic raw material
options.c: economies of scale in a small market

questions.explanation: A patent gives the inventor the sole legal right to make and sell the invention for a period, which blocks entry and creates monopoly. Option B would arise if the firm controlled an essential input. Option A is a pricing strategy a monopolist may use, not a cause of monopoly.

questions.question: A small town can support only one water-supply firm, because the cost of laying pipes means a second firm could never cover its costs. This type of monopoly arises mainly because

options.a: the firm is in perfect competition
options.b: the firm holds a patent on water
options.d: the market size does not require more than one producer, and one firm enjoys economies of scale

questions.explanation: When average cost keeps falling over the whole market's output, one large firm can supply more cheaply than two, so the market supports only one producer. Option B is wrong because water is not a patented invention. Option C is a pricing practice, not the reason only one firm exists.

questions.question: Why can a monopolist continue to earn supernormal profit in the long run, unlike a firm in perfect competition?

options.a: It faces a perfectly elastic demand curve
options.b: Barriers to entry prevent new firms from entering and competing the profit away
options.c: It produces where marginal cost is at its minimum
options.d: Its marginal revenue is always equal to its price

questions.explanation: Supernormal profit normally attracts new firms, but a monopolist's barriers to entry, such as patents, licences or control of key inputs, keep rivals out. Option D describes perfect competition; for a monopolist MR is below price. Option A also describes a perfectly competitive firm.

questions.question: For a monopolist facing a downward-sloping demand curve, marginal revenue is less than price because

options.a: to sell an extra unit it must lower the price on all the units it sells
options.b: its marginal cost is always rising
options.d: it must pay higher wages as output rises

questions.explanation: A single-price monopolist must cut price to sell more, and the lower price applies to every unit, so the extra revenue from one more unit is less than the price of that unit. Option B is about cost, not revenue. Option C is wrong because a monopolist is a price maker.

questions.question: An industry dominated by two firms whose decisions on price and output affect each other is a
questions.explanation: A duopoly has two prominent sellers who interact and are strategically interdependent. Option A also has two firms, but they are the main buyers, not sellers. Options B and D have one seller and one buyer respectively.

questions.question: In a duopoly, the quantity demanded of one firm's product depends on

options.a: both its own price and the price charged by the rival firm

questions.explanation: Because the two firms' products are close substitutes, a price change by one firm shifts buyers towards or away from the other, so demand depends on both prices. Option D ignores the rival, which is the central feature of duopoly. Options B and C leave out price competition entirely.

questions.question: Only two firms supply nearly all the cooking gas cylinders in a state. When one cuts its price, the other quickly matches it to avoid losing customers. This market is best described as a
questions.explanation: Two dominant sellers that watch and react to each other's prices form a duopoly, marked by interdependence and price competition. Option A would have only one seller. Option C would have many sellers who cannot influence price.

questions.question: A market with a small number of firms, each with significant influence on market behaviour but none able to dominate the others, is
questions.explanation: Oligopoly has a few firms whose actions all matter for the market, so none dominates and each must consider the others. Option C has one firm. Options A and D have many firms, each with little effect on the market.

questions.question: Which of the following is a key feature of oligopoly?

options.c: Interdependence, because one firm's action affects the other firms
options.d: A very large number of small firms

questions.explanation: With only a few firms, each firm's price, output or advertising decision affects its rivals, so firms must anticipate each other's reactions. Option D describes perfect or monopolistic competition. Options B and A are wrong because oligopoly has high barriers and firms set prices.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of oligopoly?

options.d: Free and easy entry of new firms

questions.explanation: Oligopoly is protected by high barriers to entry, so free and easy entry is not one of its features. Options A, B and C all describe oligopoly.

questions.question: Nigeria's mobile telecom market is served by a few large operators. Each spends heavily on advertising and quickly responds when a rival launches a new data price. This market structure is best described as
questions.explanation: A few large firms, high entry barriers such as licences and network costs, strategic advertising and reactions to rivals' prices are signs of oligopoly. Option D would have many small price-taking firms. Option B would have only one operator.

questions.question: The kinked demand curve model of oligopoly is used to explain why

options.a: prices tend to remain stable even when costs change
options.b: an oligopolist faces a horizontal demand curve

questions.explanation: The model assumes rivals match a price cut but ignore a price rise, so demand is elastic above the current price and inelastic below it. The resulting gap in the MR curve means MC can change within it without changing the profit-maximising price, so prices are sticky. Options D and B are not predictions of the model.

questions.question: An industry with many buyers and sellers whose products are differentiated but close substitutes, with free entry and exit, is
questions.explanation: Monopolistic competition combines many firms and free entry, as in perfect competition, with product differentiation, which gives each firm a little market power. Option D has identical products. Option A has only a few firms protected by barriers.

questions.question: A Lagos street has dozens of hair salons. Each offers slightly different styles, service and ambience, and new salons open easily whenever business looks good. This market is best described as
questions.explanation: Many sellers, differentiated but substitutable services and free entry are the features of monopolistic competition. Option A would have only a few dominant firms with high barriers. Option B is a market with two large buyers.

questions.question: Short-run supernormal profit in monopolistic competition tends to disappear in the long run because

options.a: it attracts new firms into the industry, which wipes away the profit
options.b: products become perfect substitutes for each other
options.d: firms are forced to merge into a monopoly

questions.explanation: Free entry means that when firms earn supernormal profit, new firms enter with similar products, demand for each firm falls, and only normal profit remains in the long run. Option D is wrong because free entry keeps the number of firms large. Option B is wrong because products remain differentiated.

questions.question: Which of the following is a feature of monopolistic competition?

options.b: Imperfect consumer knowledge of the firms' brands
options.c: Only one seller in the industry

questions.explanation: Buyers in monopolistic competition do not know everything about every brand, which helps firms use advertising, quality and branding to compete. Option C describes monopoly. Option D describes perfect competition, where products are homogeneous.

questions.question: What is the main difference between perfect competition and monopolistic competition?

options.a: Perfect competition has one buyer while monopolistic competition has many
options.b: Products are homogeneous in perfect competition but differentiated in monopolistic competition
options.c: Perfect competition has a few firms while monopolistic competition has one
options.d: Entry is free in monopolistic competition but blocked in perfect competition

questions.explanation: Both structures have many firms and free entry, but perfectly competitive firms sell identical products while monopolistically competitive firms sell differentiated close substitutes. Option C confuses the number of firms. Option D is wrong because entry is free in both.

questions.question: A market in which there is only one buyer of the goods produced by many suppliers is
questions.explanation: Monopsony means a single buyer facing many sellers, so the buyer has great power over price and quantity. Option C is a single seller facing many buyers. Option B has two large buyers.

questions.question: In a monopsony, the prices received by suppliers tend to be

options.b: high, because suppliers can choose among many buyers
options.c: low, because the single buyer has strong bargaining power
options.d: fixed at the perfectly competitive level

questions.explanation: Since sellers have no other buyer to turn to, the monopsonist can push prices down, so suppliers have low bargaining power. Option B is wrong because there is only one buyer. Option D ignores the buyer's market power.

questions.question: In a remote mining town, one mining company is the only employer of labour, and hundreds of workers have no other job options nearby. The labour market in this town is an example of
questions.explanation: A single buyer of labour facing many workers is a monopsony, and geographical location is one of its causes. Option B is about a single seller of a product, not a single buyer. Option D has two sellers.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a likely cause of monopsony?

options.a: Unregulated mergers and acquisitions among buyers
options.d: A large number of competing buyers in the market

questions.explanation: Monopsony requires a single buyer, so many competing buyers rule it out. Options C, B and A can all leave sellers facing just one buyer.

questions.question: Which of the following is a likely effect of monopsony on the market?

options.a: Free entry of many new buyers
options.b: Very high prices paid to suppliers
options.c: Perfect knowledge among all buyers and sellers
options.d: Low innovation and market inefficiency, because competition is low

questions.explanation: With only one buyer, competition is weak, which tends to reduce innovation and make the market less efficient. Option B is wrong because the single buyer pushes prices down. Option A is wrong because monopsony has barriers to entry.

questions.question: A market in which two large firms are the main buyers of the goods and services of many producers is
questions.explanation: Duopsony means two dominant buyers facing many sellers. Option D has two dominant sellers instead of buyers. Option C has only one buyer.

questions.question: In a cocoa-growing area, thousands of farmers can sell their beans only to two large processing companies, which together determine how much cocoa is bought and at what price. This market is a
questions.explanation: Two large buyers facing many sellers is a duopsony; the two firms determine market demand and enjoy strong bargaining power. Option C would have two sellers, but here the farmers are many sellers. Option A would have many buyers.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a feature of duopsony?

options.a: Low barriers to entry for new buyers
options.b: Less competition and higher profit for the two firms
options.c: The firms enjoy great bargaining power
options.d: The two firms determine market demand

questions.explanation: Duopsony is protected by high barriers to entry, so low barriers are not one of its features. Options D, C and B are all features of duopsony.

questions.question: Which pair correctly matches the market structure with its description?

options.a: Monopoly: one seller; monopsony: one buyer
options.b: Duopoly: two buyers; duopsony: two sellers
options.c: Monopoly: one buyer; monopsony: one seller
options.d: Monopsony: two buyers; duopsony: one buyer

questions.explanation: The '-poly' structures count sellers and the '-psony' structures count buyers, so monopoly is one seller and monopsony is one buyer. Option C reverses the two terms. Option B reverses duopoly (two sellers) and duopsony (two buyers).

questions.question: Which of the following is a barrier to entry that can protect firms in a monopoly or oligopoly?

options.a: Free movement of firms into and out of the industry
options.b: Homogeneous products sold by many firms
options.c: The need for a government licence to operate
options.d: Perfect knowledge of the market by all buyers

questions.explanation: A licence requirement legally limits who can operate, so it keeps potential rivals out and protects existing firms. Options D and B are features of perfect competition, where there are no barriers. Option A is the absence of barriers.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the products sold in an oligopoly?

options.a: Each firm's product has no relationship to its rivals' products
options.b: There is only one product with no substitutes
options.c: They may be homogeneous and substitutable, although product differentiation also happens
options.d: They are always perfectly identical and never branded

questions.explanation: Oligopoly products are substitutes for one another and can be fairly similar, but firms often differentiate them through branding and advertising. Option D is too strict, since differentiation does happen. Option B describes monopoly.

questions.question: Apart from economies of scale and legal barriers, which of the following can put a monopolist in a superior position in its industry?

options.a: Access to market intelligence or technology that other firms cannot obtain
options.b: Having no control over the price of its product
options.c: Selling a product that has many close substitutes
options.d: Facing a perfectly elastic demand curve

questions.explanation: A monopolist often has unique information or technology that rivals cannot get, which strengthens its hold on the market. Option C would weaken monopoly power, since buyers could switch. Options B and D describe a price taker in perfect competition.

questions.question: Normal profit is best described as

options.b: the minimum profit needed to keep a firm in its present industry, earned when total revenue just covers total cost including opportunity cost
options.c: any profit above the level needed to keep the firm in the industry

questions.explanation: Normal profit is the return that just keeps the entrepreneur in the industry, so economic profit is zero when TR equals TC including opportunity cost. Option C defines supernormal (abnormal) profit. Option A ignores variable cost.

questions.question: A perfectly competitive sachet-water producer sells at the market price of N250 per bag. If it sells 640 bags, what are its total revenue and its marginal revenue per bag?
questions.explanation: TR = P x Q = 250 x 640 = N160,000, and since a price taker can sell each extra bag at the same N250, MR = P = N250. Option D assumes extra sales add no revenue. Option B halves the price, as for a straight-line monopoly demand curve, which does not apply to a price taker.

questions.question: A monopolist's demand schedule is: Quantity 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 units; Price N900, N800, N700, N600, N500, N400 respectively. What is the total revenue at 4 units?
questions.explanation: Total revenue = price x quantity = 600 x 4 = N2,400. Option B is the price (average revenue) at 4 units, not the total. Option C is the marginal revenue of the 4th unit (2,400 - 2,100).

questions.question: A monopolist's demand schedule is: Quantity 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 units; Price N900, N800, N700, N600, N500, N400 respectively. What is the marginal revenue of the 3rd unit?
questions.explanation: MR = TR(3) - TR(2) = (700 x 3) - (800 x 2) = 2,100 - 1,600 = N500. Option A is the price of the 3rd unit; MR is lower because the price cut applies to all units sold. Option C is total revenue at 3 units.

questions.question: A monopolist's demand schedule is: Quantity 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 units; Price N900, N800, N700, N600, N500, N400 respectively. At what output is the monopolist's total revenue at its maximum?
questions.explanation: TR is N900, N1,600, N2,100, N2,400, N2,500 and N2,400, so it peaks at 5 units, where MR is still positive (N100) and the next unit has negative MR (-N100). Option B is wrong because the 6th unit lowers TR. Option A has the highest price but the lowest revenue.

questions.question: A monopolist's demand schedule is: Quantity 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 units; Price N900, N800, N700, N600, N500, N400 respectively. What is the average revenue at 5 units?
questions.explanation: Average revenue = TR / Q = 2,500 / 5 = N500, which equals the price at that output, as it always does when one price is charged. Option D is the marginal revenue of the 5th unit (N100). Option A is total revenue.

questions.question: A monopolist's demand schedule is: Quantity 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 units; Price N900, N800, N700, N600, N500, N400 respectively. Its fixed cost is N400 and the marginal costs of units 1 to 6 are N300, N200, N250, N280, N400, N500 respectively. What output maximises the monopolist's profit?
questions.explanation: Marginal revenues are N900, N700, N500, N300, N100 and -N100. The 4th unit adds N300 to revenue but only N280 to cost, while every later unit adds more to cost than to revenue, so profit is highest at 4 units. Option A is the revenue-maximising output, where the 5th unit adds N100 of revenue but N400 of cost. Option C is where MC is lowest, which is not the profit rule.

questions.question: A monopolist's demand schedule is: Quantity 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 units; Price N900, N800, N700, N600, N500, N400 respectively.
